notes.definition: Waste management is the safe handling and disposal of the waste and chemical materials produced by humans. Rapid growth in the human population and a higher standard of living mean more resources are used and more waste is produced, which causes pollution unless it is properly handled.
explanation: The human population has grown very rapidly, from about 1 billion people in 1800 to about 8 billion today. At the same time, the standard of living in many countries has increased: people own more goods, use more energy, eat more processed food and travel more. Both changes mean that more resources (such as fossil fuels, minerals, food and water) are used and more waste is produced. Unless waste and chemical materials are properly handled, more pollution will be caused.

Pollution can occur in water. Sewage, fertiliser that runs off farmland and toxic chemicals from industry can enter rivers, lakes and seas. Toxic chemicals can poison aquatic organisms directly. Sewage and fertiliser add extra nutrients to the water, which can cause rapid growth of algae; the algae block light from water plants, and when organisms die, decomposing microorganisms use up oxygen in the water, so fish and other animals die.

Pollution can occur in air. Burning fuels produces smoke, which contains tiny solid particles, and acidic gases such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Smoke can reduce the light reaching plants and harm the lungs of animals. Acidic gases dissolve in water in the atmosphere to form acid rain, which can damage the leaves of trees and make lakes and rivers too acidic for many organisms to survive.

Pollution can occur on land. Landfill sites, where waste is buried, take up land that could have been habitat for plants and animals. Toxic chemicals, such as some pesticides, herbicides and chemicals that leak from landfill or industrial sites, can contaminate the soil and kill organisms. Some toxic chemicals can also wash into water from the land.

Pollution kills plants and animals, which can reduce biodiversity. When sensitive species die, the species that depend on them for food or shelter are affected too. Handling waste properly, for example treating sewage before it is released, controlling the use of fertilisers and pesticides, filtering waste gases, and reducing, reusing and recycling materials instead of sending them to landfill, reduces pollution and helps to protect biodiversity.
keyFacts: Rapid human population growth and a higher standard of living mean more resources are used and more waste is produced.
Unless waste and chemical materials are properly handled, more pollution will be caused.
Water pollution can come from sewage, fertiliser or toxic chemicals.
Air pollution can come from smoke and acidic gases.
Land pollution can come from landfill and from toxic chemicals.
Pollution kills plants and animals, which can reduce biodiversity.
Acidic gases such as sulfur dioxide can cause acid rain.
Recycling and proper treatment of waste reduce pollution.

keyTerms.definition: The release of harmful substances or energy into the environment, which can harm or kill living organisms.
The level of wealth and comfort that people have, including the goods and services they use.
Waste water containing human faeces and urine, plus water from washing and industry.
A substance containing mineral ions such as nitrates and phosphates, added to soil to help crops grow.
Gases such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, released when fuels burn, which dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain.
A site where waste is buried in the ground.
A substance that is poisonous to living organisms, such as some pesticides and industrial chemicals.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think pollution is only caused by factories.
misconceptions.right: In fact, pollution comes from many sources, including sewage from homes, fertiliser from farms, smoke from burning fuels and household waste in landfill.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fertiliser cannot be a pollutant because it helps plants grow.
misconceptions.right: In fact, fertiliser that runs into water can cause rapid growth of algae; the resulting lack of light and oxygen kills water plants and animals.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think more waste is produced only because there are more people.
misconceptions.right: In fact, a higher standard of living also increases the resources used and waste produced per person.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think acid rain is caused by carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.right: In fact, acid rain is mainly caused by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Carbon dioxide is linked to global warming.

realWorld: Sewage treatment works remove solids and harmful microorganisms from waste water before it is released into rivers.
Power stations fit equipment to remove sulfur dioxide from waste gases, which has greatly reduced acid rain in the UK since the 1980s.
Councils run kerbside recycling collections to reduce the amount of waste that goes to landfill.
Farmers are advised not to spread fertiliser close to rivers or before heavy rain, to reduce run-off into water.
examTips: Learn the three places pollution can occur (water, air, land) and the sources AQA lists for each.
Always link pollution to its effect on biodiversity: pollution kills plants and animals, which can reduce biodiversity.
Give both reasons for more waste: rapid population growth and an increase in the standard of living.
When reading population graphs, check the units on the axis (for example billions) and include them in your answer.
Do not confuse acid rain (sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides) with global warming (carbon dioxide, methane).
summary: Population growth and higher standards of living mean more resources are used and more waste is produced.
Waste must be handled properly or pollution increases.
Pollution kills plants and animals and can reduce biodiversity.

questions.question: Which of these is a source of water pollution named in the AQA specification?
markScheme: 1 mark: sewage
questions.explanation: Sewage, fertiliser and toxic chemicals pollute water. Smoke and acidic gases pollute air, and landfill pollutes land.

questions.question: Which of these causes air pollution?
markScheme: 1 mark: smoke
questions.explanation: Smoke and acidic gases are air pollutants. Fertiliser and sewage are water pollutants; landfill pollutes land.

questions.question: Which two factors mean that more waste is being produced?
options: More people and a higher standard of living
Fewer people and a lower standard of living
markScheme: 1 mark: more people and a higher standard of living
questions.explanation: Rapid population growth and an increase in the standard of living both increase the resources used and the waste produced.

questions.question: How does pollution affect biodiversity?
options: It increases biodiversity by adding nutrients
It has no effect on biodiversity
It can reduce biodiversity by killing plants and animals
markScheme: 1 mark: it can reduce biodiversity by killing plants and animals
questions.explanation: The AQA specification states that pollution kills plants and animals, which can reduce biodiversity.

questions.question: Which gas released from burning fossil fuels is a main cause of acid rain?
markScheme: 1 mark: sulfur dioxide
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form an acidic solution. Methane is a greenhouse gas, and oxygen and nitrogen are not acidic gases.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of land pollution?
options: Toxic chemicals leaking from a landfill site into soil
markScheme: 1 mark: toxic chemicals leaking from landfill into soil
questions.explanation: Landfill and toxic chemicals pollute land. Fertiliser in a river is water pollution and smoke and sulfur dioxide are air pollution.

questions.question: Fertiliser runs into a lake. Which sequence of events most likely follows?
options: Fewer algae, more light, more oxygen, more fish
Algae grow rapidly, water plants die from lack of light, decomposers use up oxygen, fish die
The water becomes acidic and fish grow faster
The lake freezes over, so fish die
markScheme: 1 mark: algae grow rapidly, plants die, decomposers use oxygen, fish die
questions.explanation: Extra nutrients cause algae to grow quickly and block light. Dead organisms are decomposed by microorganisms, which use up dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate.

questions.question: A river was tested above and below a sewage outflow. Which result would show that the sewage was polluting the river?
options: Higher oxygen concentration below the outflow
More species of invertebrate below the outflow
Lower oxygen concentration and fewer invertebrate species below the outflow
No difference between the two sites
markScheme: 1 mark: lower oxygen and fewer invertebrate species below the outflow
questions.explanation: Microorganisms decomposing sewage use up oxygen, so fewer species can survive below the outflow. More oxygen and more species would suggest cleaner water.

questions.question: Which measure would most directly reduce acid rain?
options: Removing sulfur dioxide from power station waste gases
markScheme: 1 mark: removing sulfur dioxide from power station waste gases
questions.explanation: Acid rain is caused by acidic gases such as sulfur dioxide, so removing them at the source reduces acid rain. The other measures reduce different types of pollution.

questions.question:

questions.explanation: 210 ÷ 600 = 0.35, so 35% of the waste was recycled.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the mass of waste sent to landfill by a council before and after a recycling scheme started.
Calculate the percentage decrease in the mass of waste sent to landfill.

headers: Mass of waste sent to landfill in tonnes

questions.explanation: The decrease is 28 000 tonnes. 28 000 ÷ 80 000 = 0.35, so the decrease is 35%.

questions.question:
A city of 250 000 people produces a mean of 1.2 kg of household waste per person per day.
Calculate the total mass of household waste produced by the city in one day.
Give your answer in tonnes.
1 tonne = 1000 kg
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of people by the waste per person, then convert kilograms to tonnes by dividing by 1000.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the world population in 1800 and in 2020.
Calculate the mean increase in population per year over this period.
Give your answer in millions of people per year.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 6.8 billion over 220 years
1 mark: 6.8 ÷ 220 = 0.0309 billion = 30.9 million per year
questions.explanation: 6 800 million ÷ 220 years = 30.9 million per year. Note that the real growth was much slower at the start and much faster in recent decades, so a mean hides the pattern.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the world population in 1950 and in 2020.
Calculate the percentage increase in the world population between 1950 and 2020.
questions.explanation: 5.3 ÷ 2.5 = 2.12, which is a 212% increase. The population more than tripled.

questions.question: Give one reason why the amount of waste produced by humans is increasing.
markScheme: 1 mark: rapid growth in human population or an increase in the standard of living
questions.explanation: Either reason is credited: more people, or each person using more resources.

questions.question: Name two substances that can pollute water.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: sewage; fertiliser; toxic chemicals (for example pesticides)
questions.explanation: AQA lists sewage, fertiliser and toxic chemicals as water pollutants.

questions.question: Name one type of pollution caused by landfill sites.
markScheme: 1 mark: land pollution / toxic chemicals leaking into soil or water / takes up land (habitat)
questions.explanation: Landfill is a source of land pollution; chemicals can also leak out and the site itself removes habitat.

questions.question: Explain how acidic gases released by burning fuels can reduce biodiversity in a lake.
markScheme: 1 mark: acidic gases (such as sulfur dioxide) dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain
1 mark: the lake becomes too acidic, so sensitive organisms die and fewer species survive
questions.explanation: Acid rain lowers the pH of lakes, killing organisms that cannot tolerate acidic water and reducing the number of species.

questions.question: Explain why an increase in the standard of living leads to more pollution, even if the population stays the same.
markScheme: 1 mark: each person uses more resources (goods, energy, food, transport)
1 mark: so more waste is produced (or more fuel is burned), which causes more pollution unless properly handled
questions.explanation: A higher standard of living increases consumption per person, so total waste rises even if the number of people does not.

questions.question: Describe two ways in which toxic chemicals can enter the environment and harm organisms.
markScheme: 1 mark: a named route, for example pesticides or herbicides sprayed on crops, chemicals leaking from landfill, industrial waste released into rivers
1 mark: a second route, or how they harm organisms: they poison and kill plants and animals in soil or water
questions.explanation: Toxic chemicals can pollute both land and water and kill organisms directly.

questions.question: Explain how untreated sewage released into a river can lead to the death of fish.
markScheme: 1 mark: sewage adds nutrients, causing rapid growth of algae (which block light so water plants die)
1 mark: microorganisms (bacteria) decompose the sewage and dead organisms
1 mark: decomposers use up dissolved oxygen, so fish die from lack of oxygen
questions.explanation: The key link is that respiration by decomposers removes oxygen from the water faster than it is replaced.

questions.question:
A scientist counted the number of invertebrate species in a stream above and below a farm.
Table 1 shows the results.
Suggest an explanation for the results.
markScheme: 1 mark: fertiliser, pesticides or animal waste from the farm ran off into the stream
1 mark: this pollution killed organisms (directly or by reducing oxygen), so fewer species survived below the farm
questions.explanation: The difference points to pollution entering the stream from the farm, reducing biodiversity downstream.

questions.question: Describe the different ways in which humans pollute water, air and land.
markScheme: Indicative content: water: sewage, fertiliser run-off, toxic chemicals from industry or pesticides; air: smoke from burning fuels, acidic gases such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (acid rain); land: landfill sites, toxic chemicals such as pesticides and herbicides, chemicals leaking from waste; effect: kills plants and animals, reducing biodiversity.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): sources of pollution described for all three of water, air and land, with some effects on organisms.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two sources named with little description.
questions.explanation: A full answer covers all three areas from the specification and links them to the death of organisms.

questions.question:
The human population is increasing rapidly and the standard of living is rising in many countries.
Explain how these changes can lead to a reduction in biodiversity through pollution, and describe how waste can be managed to reduce this effect.
markScheme: Indicative content: more people and higher standard of living mean more resources used and more waste produced; unless properly handled, more pollution; water pollution from sewage, fertiliser and toxic chemicals (algal growth, oxygen depletion, poisoning); air pollution from smoke and acidic gases (acid rain damages trees and acidifies lakes); land pollution from landfill and toxic chemicals (loss of habitat, poisoning); pollution kills plants and animals, which reduces biodiversity; knock-on effects on food webs.

Management: treat sewage before release; control fertiliser and pesticide use, avoid spreading near rivers; filter or remove sulfur dioxide from waste gases; reduce, reuse and recycle to reduce landfill; safe disposal of toxic chemicals; line and monitor landfill sites.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear causal chain from population and living standards to pollution in water, air and land, explicit link to reduced biodiversity, and several specific management methods.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some sources and effects of pollution explained, with at least one management method.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about more waste or pollution with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The best answers link cause to effect step by step and match management methods to particular types of pollution.

questions.question: Why can landfill sites reduce biodiversity even if no toxic chemicals leak from them?
options: They take up land that could be a habitat for plants and animals
They increase the oxygen content of soil
markScheme: 1 mark: they take up land that could be habitat
questions.explanation: Using land for dumping waste reduces the land available for other organisms.

questions.question: State one way that a household can reduce the amount of waste it sends to landfill.
markScheme: 1 mark: recycle / reuse / reduce what is bought / compost food waste
questions.explanation: Reducing, reusing and recycling all cut the amount of waste that ends up in landfill.
